title: FamilySearch Full-Text Search and Transkribus make handwritten records searchable, and a genealogist uses Full-Text Search to transcribe a 1761 deed
summary: FamilySearch Full-Text Search converts handwritten records into searchable text, and a genealogist used it to help transcribe a 1761 deed; Transkribus claims 200 million pages deciphered.
account: FamilySearch introduced Full-Text Search through FamilySearch Labs in 2024. The feature uses handwriting recognition and optical character recognition. Transkribus, developed by the European cooperative READ-COOP SCE, says on its site that it “turns centuries of handwriting into text you can search, study, and share”. It claims over 500,000 users and 200 million pages deciphered. It cites projects such as the University of Georgia transcribing 20,000 pages in two months and Archion's portal of over 200,000 German church books. Historians at Wilfrid Laurier University measured Transkribus on 50 pages of 18th and 19th century English handwriting (arXiv, 2 November 2024; Historical Methods, 26 May 2025). The two Transkribus models read 90 to 92% of characters and 73 to 80% of words correctly, and commercial large language models did better. The newsroom of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reviewed FamilySearch's year 2024 on 2 January 2025. It says that FamilySearch “can convert an image of text into a machine-readable text format, allowing users to search the full text of the records”. It reports that 2.5 billion searchable records and images were added overall in 2024. It gives no example of a user discovery. FamilySearch's year-end review for 2025, reproduced on 9 January 2026, says that Full-Text Search was fully released from FamilySearch Labs in 2025, alongside 2.2 billion newly searchable names and images. Its plans for 2026, reported on 13 January 2026, are to extend the handwriting-reading technology to additional languages. On 26 October 2026 the genealogist Randy Seaver published a 1761 deed of an ancestor that he had transcribed with help from FamilySearch Full-Text Search, with a few errors corrected. No independent source documents a specific discovery, reunion or entitlement from either system.
purpose: Make handwritten historical records searchable by converting images to text with AI handwriting recognition
system: FamilySearch Full-Text Search (handwriting recognition and OCR); Transkribus (READ-COOP SCE)

location: Global (FamilySearch users; European and US archives)

evidence.citation: Humphries M, Leddy LC, Downton Q, Legace M, McConnell J, Murray I, Spence E. Unlocking the Archives: Large Language Models Achieve State-of-the-Art Performance on the Transcription of Handwritten Historical Documents. arXiv 2411.03340, 2 November 2024; published as "Unlocking the archives: Using large language models to transcribe handwritten historical documents" in Historical Methods 58(3):175-193, 26 May 2025 (doi:10.1080/01615440.2025.2500309). The authors are historians at Wilfrid Laurier University, funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, and they declare no competing interests; they built a competing open-source tool that uses commercial LLMs. They found that the two Transkribus models read 90 to 92% of characters and 73 to 80% of words correctly on 18th and 19th century English handwriting, and that LLMs did better.
evidence.title: Unlocking the Archives: Large Language Models Achieve State-of-the-Art Performance on the Transcription of Handwritten Historical Documents
evidence.quote: This means that on the task of achieving a perfect transcription, the Transkribus models correctly transcribed between 90 and 92% of the characters and 73 and 80% of the words in the ground truth document.

evidence.citation: Seaver R. Amanuensis Monday -- 1761 Deed of Benjamin Wing Buying Land in Dartmouth, Bristol County, Massachusetts Bay Colony From Samuel Wait. Genea-Musings, 26 October 2026. Seaver is a genealogist and a FamilySearch user, and Benjamin Wing is one of his ancestors; his post states that he transcribed the deed with help from Full-Text Search and corrected a few errors.

evidence.citation: Humphries M, Leddy LC, Downton Q, Legace M, McConnell J, Murray I, Spence E. Unlocking the Archives: Large Language Models Achieve State-of-the-Art Performance on the Transcription of Handwritten Historical Documents. arXiv 2411.03340, 2 November 2024; published as "Unlocking the archives: Using large language models to transcribe handwritten historical documents" in Historical Methods 58(3):175-193, 26 May 2025 (doi:10.1080/01615440.2025.2500309). The authors are historians at Wilfrid Laurier University, funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, and they declare no competing interests; they built a competing open-source tool that uses commercial LLMs. They found that the two Transkribus models read 90 to 92% of characters and 73 to 80% of words correctly on 18th and 19th century English handwriting, and that LLMs did better.
evidence.title: Unlocking the Archives: Large Language Models Achieve State-of-the-Art Performance on the Transcription of Handwritten Historical Documents
evidence.quote: This means that on the task of achieving a perfect transcription, the Transkribus models correctly transcribed between 90 and 92% of the characters and 73 and 80% of the words in the ground truth document.

evidence.citation: Seaver R. Amanuensis Monday -- 1761 Deed of Benjamin Wing Buying Land in Dartmouth, Bristol County, Massachusetts Bay Colony From Samuel Wait. Genea-Musings, 26 October 2026. Seaver is a genealogist and a FamilySearch user, and Benjamin Wing is one of his ancestors; his post states that he transcribed the deed with help from Full-Text Search and corrected a few errors.

display.answer: The Church newsroom and the Transkribus site are the makers' own pages, and the Genea-Musings post of 13 January 2026 reproduces FamilySearch's announcement. The accuracy study comes from historians at Wilfrid Laurier University who declare no competing interests and who built a competing tool. The post of 26 October 2026 comes from a genealogist who used Full-Text Search.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: FamilySearch Full-Text Search converts handwritten records into searchable text, and a genealogist used it to help transcribe a 1761 deed; Transkribus claims 200 million pages deciphered.
fields.account: FamilySearch introduced Full-Text Search through FamilySearch Labs in 2024. The feature uses handwriting recognition and optical character recognition. Transkribus, developed by the European cooperative READ-COOP SCE, says on its site that it “turns centuries of handwriting into text you can search, study, and share”. It claims over 500,000 users and 200 million pages deciphered. It cites projects such as the University of Georgia transcribing 20,000 pages in two months and Archion's portal of over 200,000 German church books. Historians at Wilfrid Laurier University measured Transkribus on 50 pages of 18th and 19th century English handwriting (arXiv, 2 November 2024; Historical Methods, 26 May 2025). The two Transkribus models read 90 to 92% of characters and 73 to 80% of words correctly, and commercial large language models did better. The newsroom of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reviewed FamilySearch's year 2024 on 2 January 2025. It says that FamilySearch “can convert an image of text into a machine-readable text format, allowing users to search the full text of the records”. It reports that 2.5 billion searchable records and images were added overall in 2024. It gives no example of a user discovery. FamilySearch's year-end review for 2025, reproduced on 9 January 2026, says that Full-Text Search was fully released from FamilySearch Labs in 2025, alongside 2.2 billion newly searchable names and images. Its plans for 2026, reported on 13 January 2026, are to extend the handwriting-reading technology to additional languages. On 26 October 2026 the genealogist Randy Seaver published a 1761 deed of an ancestor that he had transcribed with help from FamilySearch Full-Text Search, with a few errors corrected. No independent source documents a specific discovery, reunion or entitlement from either system.
